title: DI and di: Why They Are Not the Same and Why That Matters
author: Daniel Muijs
summary: Daniel Muijs, a long-time researcher of teacher effectiveness, separates Direct Instruction, the scripted programme designed by Engelmann, from direct instruction, the broader approach exemplified by Rosenshine's principles. Each rests on its own body of research: Project Follow Through and later quasi-experimental studies for DI, and classroom-observation studies from the teacher effectiveness tradition for di. Both build on explicit instruction, but DI is fully scripted while di is a set of principles the teacher interprets and adapts. Muijs argues the difference positions the teacher entirely differently, as a deliverer of prepared instruction in one case and as a professional shaping their own lessons in the other. He grants that scripting can lift poor teaching to adequate, but says great teaching needs teacher agency, contextual adaptation and variety, including recognition of the expertise-reversal effect. His conclusion is that the curriculum, not a script, should guide the teacher.
points: Direct Instruction (scripted, Engelmann) and direct instruction (Rosenshine-style principles) are different things with different evidence bases, and conflating them confuses the debate.
A fully scripted approach can raise poor teaching to adequate and prevent misguided practice, but it caps what teachers can achieve because teaching is relational and contextual.

Direct instruction is the necessary approach for novices, yet the expertise-reversal effect means experts need something different, so teaching must vary as pupils move along the novice-expert continuum.
The teacher's guide should be the curriculum, meaning the knowledge and skills pupils are to acquire, rather than a script.
Evidence-informed practice should feature plenty of di but not always and not everywhere, with teachers adapting to what, who and where they teach.
quotes: The distinction is crucial, as it ultimately positions the teacher in an entirely different way. The teacher following Engelmann’s DI is essentially a deliverer of instruction prepared elsewhere. The teacher following Rosenshine’s principles is a professional shaping what happens in their own lessons.
But while DI is a fully scripted approach, di is more a set of principles that are open to interpretation and adaptation by the teacher.
All teaching is relational, in that it occurs in a dialogue between the teacher and the pupils in that class.
While di is the necessary approach for novice learners, we know that the expertise-reversal effect means that it is not so for experts (Sweller, 2024).

A scripted approach can improve outcomes, especially where teaching is poor in the first place. But in the absence of teacher agency and professionalism this will only ever elevate us from poor to adequate.
The guide for the teacher needs to be the curriculum, not a script. What knowledge and skills do I want my pupils to acquire, and how do I do that?
A lesson should be a river that flows towards its goal in sometimes unexpected directions, not a canal constrained by rigid walls.
